utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will rise for 10 minutes. --- Break taken at 11.20 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a couple of questions. If we could have 354 in e-court, and I have to ask that this not be broadcast. And I want to go to page 7, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, can we -- my colleague explain what he is going to do before he does it. Because I believe that this is beyond the scope of cross-examination and I may be -- maybe it is, but I would like him to explain what exactly he is going to try to do with a document that was not used. If he can do it before we ask the question so we can avoid any interruptions once the witness begins to answer. And maybe the witness should remove his earphones while we have this discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think I should be able to just go ahead and the objection could be when I start asking the questions, but I can explain it, and the witness remove his headphones if I'm going to explain it. I don't object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you kindly do that. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There have been questions on cross-examination about when this date was, what time the witness was at the check-point and back at the brigade headquarters and who was in command on that day, who was meeting with Beara and Popovic that day, which commander. And there's been talk and questions about that it was Obrenovic standing in for Pandurevic, the witness has said he wasn't at meeting. What I intend to do is show him the Zvornik Brigade military policemen's duty roster. That roster shows the assignments, or it's got a log of where the military policemen were during the month of July. And on this witness's name there is evidence that there was an R on the 15th of July, which was then poorly erased, and a T, standing for terrain, was substituted for it. And that goes not just for this witness but other MPs who were at Rocevic on the 15th of July, 1995. So I want to show the witness that roster, get his comment on it and see if it refreshes his memory. Before the witness began testifying we went over this in -- yesterday a bit. He said always that these events took place shortly after the fall of Srebrenica and then he said he wasn't sure when that fall was and the date. So I think now the issue of what date this was when he was in the command and heard about this meeting, I can show him this roster and see if that helps him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't believe, Mr. President, this is not a question that should be allowed. This is a question that came out in direct examination. There were many questions asked, many attempts by the left, by the right, by the back, by the front, and every time, he got 11th or I don't recall. At that time this document is a document that was in his possession. He could have shown his exhibit to the witness, asked the witness the question, and checked whether the -- where was the witness that day. Now, in cross-examination no one asked the witness about the particular date of these events. No one asked about that. All the questions were related to a meeting that took place, to events that took place in Rocevic, but never to a specific date. This is beyond the scope of cross-examination. It is something that my friend is probably trying to repair direct examination which is a failure, but that's his problem, it's not ours, and it should not be allowed, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just add. I concur with that objection. I also believe that it's inappropriate because I don't believe from my recollection that anyone referenced a date or whether it was after or before. And from this witness's testimony, I do object to counsel trying to shape the testimony now to suggest that he always said it was after. I think the testimony speaks for itself, as well as his summary of whether he actually felt someone was at a meeting or not at the meeting. His testimony should stand. The document should have been used if counsel wanted him to pin-point the date. It was not used in any of his meetings, it was not used during the direct, it's outside the scope of cross-examination by every stretch. I think it's highly inappropriate and very prejudicial at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, your objection is not based upon the fact that this document was not listed --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- in the 65 ter or in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Not at all. It's a Prosecution exhibit. He can use whatever exhibit he. Wants that's not the issue here. The issue is it's his witness, it was an issue that he wanted to get from the witness, he did ask the question, he was not satisfied with the answer. He asked more questions, he was still not satisfied. We had to go to get a ruling from the Chamber to get more questions, and in the end we have two things on the record: the 11th, or, "I don't recall." Now, in cross-examination, the issue doesn't come up at all, nobody discussed the date. If we had not been satisfied with the date or something, we might have cross-examined on this issue, but nobody did. Now he comes back in re-examination, tries to repair what is missing, according to him, in his case and he wants to get it at this stage. It's highly improper. That's the -- what's important about my objection. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's not just the date. Maybe I didn't explain it adequately. The thrust of a lot of the cross has been that Vinko Pandurevic was absent at this time and that the meeting must have been with the Chief of Staff, somebody standing in for him, Obrenovic, because he was not there. The witness did not see that meeting was told this meeting was with the commander. There is evidence we have and that we will be putting on that Vinko Pandurevic was there on the evening of the 15th, that he had come back, and that he was present. Therefore, that, without them saying 15th, they have, on cross-examination, tried to cement in the period of time as definitely a period of time when Pandurevic was absent. And there's going to be other evidence. I'm not going to ask this witness if he knows the exact dates of Pandurevic's coming and going. But I think it's fair to put this to him to see whether, on the date of this meeting, the date he went to Rocevic, could have been the 15th. Because that is when Pandurevic is back at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the -- what my colleague is trying to do at this time is to try and ask something that is related to the date of the events the witness testified about. That's what he's trying to get. The reference from yesterday, page 57, lines 19 to 25, page 58, lines 1 to 7, where we talk about the date. The date of the events is solved, and what he is trying to do by the back door is to get something else that is not -- unrelated to this witness. And if he wanted to do it, the time to do it was on examination-in-chief and not after cross-examination once this witness is over. It's not the proper time to raise this objection and to try and re-examine on this specific topic. If my friend later on wants to lead evidence about other events, he can do that. But with this witness, I believe this is an improper question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Briefly, sorry. I object to the assertion that I'm trying to do anything by the back door. What I'm trying to do is deal with the cross-examination of who was commander that day. The prior testimony about the date was somewhat blurry and I left it at that. However, they, on cross-examination, my friends, have cemented with the witness that this was the day when Pandurevic was not there and that the commander was standing in for him. That is what opens the door for showing him this log.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, the Chamber is of the view that the Prosecution will be allowed to put question in relation to documents as for the absence or presence of Accused Pandurevic at the time. But we agree with the points raised by Bourgon as for the date when the witness was in Rocevic. So put specific questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The problem, Mr. President, he wants to use a roster with the presence of the witness. That's the -- that's the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a separate matter. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'd like to do, Your Honours, if I may, is this is 65 ter number 354. I've got the original, which is what I intend to show the witness. And I'm just not clear on the Court's order. Am I permitted to show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- the witness the roster?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The duty roster which is related to Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. That's -- what I was going to show the witness is the duty roster relating to him and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was not clear enough. No, that's not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It hasn't appeared in the e-court yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There won't be any document used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The day you were on that -- on duty at the Rocevic School, did you know where Pandurevic was at midday that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you know where he was the evening the day you were at the Rocevic School?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At -- in the evening I was at headquarters, but I didn't know where Pandurevic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you recall - and I want to ask you to think carefully and specifically - when you were -- when you -- who -- when you were told that there was a meeting with the commander, were you given the name of that commander who was meeting with Popovic and the person you were told was Beara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-165 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't told the name. And for the first time in the statement when we discussed this, I said I was talking with the commander, but as we didn't agree with the English and Serbian version, it was written, "Commander Pandurevic," but Obrenovic was actually replacing him at that time, but I think we solved that problem with the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think I'll leave it at that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think there's more appropriate witnesses who can deal with this, but, Witness, can you answer the question -- can you explain the relation between the security officers and military police? Are military police subordinated to the security line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we personally, with the security officers, did not talk to the security officers while we were on duty. We might have sat around with them, but we received commands from the military police commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So when you said earlier that Jasikovic must have received his orders from his superior, what superior did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the chain of command was like this: The military police commander received orders from his security officer, the security officer received orders from the main commander, and that way up and down the chain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Witness. And I thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. And now you may go. And I hope you have a good trip back to your country.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we deal with the exhibits, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have just three, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P02495, the pseudonym sheet under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you tender the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No problem. Yes. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P02495, that is the pseudonym sheet under seal. P02494 is the unmarked map of the Rocevic area which I showed the witness. And 00083 in court -- PIC00083, excuse me, and that is the marked map of the Rocevic area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections? Thank you. And I have a list from the Popovic Defence. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We handed in our list to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I have it in front of me. According to the list, you are proposing to submit part of the statement and the supplemental information sheet dated 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, I absolutely object to parting out the statements. I think the Court's ruled on that before. There is no reason to do that. The parts he read out and shown are either on the record, what he read out, and he can either put in the statement or not. But these redactions and parts, I don't think, make any sense, and therefore I object to item 1. I do not object to item 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, do you have any response to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I consider that the objection is unfounded because it was the ruling of the Chamber that exhibits can be tendered into evidence only if they were shown to the witness, put to the witness and I put to the witness just that portion of the statement that I am tendering, nothing more than that. So that's all I'm asking for. That's all I want to have admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, in support of this argument, it was mentioned before, and I argued previously, that when the time comes to seek to admit portions of a statement or a full statement for the sake of credibility or impeachment purposes or for purposes other than the truth or the evidence, that it is not for the Prosecution to say what the Defence should or should not tender into evidence. The idea is for the Defence to say what is required to assist the Trial Chamber in order to determine whether a witness has or does not have credibility. In this case my colleague is asking for parts of a statement. It's -- he will have to live with his decision of putting in all or not all of it, because he feels that this is what the Chamber will require and this is what will assist the Chamber. And this is not something that the Prosecution should even get involved in. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There is this kind of code of procedure that -- that I learn about every day from Mr. Bourgon. I mean, I think it's absolutely crazy that the Prosecution is not allowed to object or make arguments on what the Defence or any other -- or what either party wishes to put in. If I try to put something in, he can make his objection and his argument. If the Defence tries to put in something, I am perfectly entitled to argue why or why not I agree with that. The rule in every other case I have tried here or anywhere else, is that when a witness is confronted with a statement or shown a statement on cross-examination, either the statement comes in or the record is relied upon and what was read from the statement. It's very artificial to parse a statement apart. And again, there is no jury here. If the Trial Chamber receives the statement they can see these extracted parts in context, and they will know what they are seeing. There is no reason to hide parts of statement from the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber knows the purpose that the statement is being submitted for, and -- and I strongly object to putting in parts of it. If necessary, I would ask that we end up briefing this because I think it's an important issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My colleague for the Prosecution, they don't have the same opinion. They express different opinions at different times. They want this trial to be a -- to be conducted according to a contradictory system when it suits them, and when it doesn't suit them, then they don't want it. They want a different system. They should pick and choose and live with their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't -- leave it at that. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My only comment is, could the Chamber please look at these -- these examples on a case-by-case basis and my slight concern about what my learned friend Mr. Nicholls is saying is he wants it argued as a matter of principle. That's a completely different issue. As far as a case-by-case issue is concerned, as is obvious, we are neutral so far as this is concerned. But there has been an occasion in the past, Chamber might recall, where I had a specific objection because of something that was contained in the statement that hadn't been cross-examined upon at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That is helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa, I didn't recognise you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like it to be noted that we object to admitting the whole statement. And we agree with our learned colleague Zivanovic that only extracts, not the whole statement, should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In light of these interventions on the part of the Defence, can I ask Mr. Zivanovic whether it is really necessary to tender these parts, only six lines in total, which was put to the witness and which was recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is what I assessed to be beneficial to my client and what I generally put to this witness. By the way, let me just remind everyone that on earlier occasions I proposed only portions of statements to be admitted, and that the Chamber granted my request. In a previous case of intercept, there was an objection from the Prosecution, but the Trial Chamber agreed just for the portion relating to my client to be admitted. So that is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I remember that. But when there were cases in which the Chamber recommended the parties to tender all the document, for the purpose of understanding the context of that paragraph, so that -- in that case, the other paragraphs are not tendered into evidence, just for the -- it was tendered to help the Chamber to understand the real evidence. So I take it that you are not tendering item 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I didn't understand what you mean, I'm not proposing Exhibit Number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was confused with your statement that, "That is what I assessed to be beneficial to my client." So you stand by your motion to tender only part of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My motion was to admit only item 11 and the first two sentences from item 12 of this statement. That was my motion. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On a separate note, have you prepared that part to be tendered into e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have instructed my team or supporting staff to do that, however I don't know if it's already been done or not. But I do expect it to be finalised any time soon now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, I'm going to withdraw this portion of the statement, and I don't bother to -- want to bother the Chamber any longer with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that resolves the matter. Thank you. So we will admit item 2 and -- which is -- which should be under seal. Thank you. And Mr. Bourgon, you are tendering two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. Two exhibits: IC84, which was a map which was initially produced by the Prosecution and which was marked by the witness. And the second item is IC85, a sketch of Rocevic School which was produced by the Defence and also marked by the witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there is no objection from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. I take it this is the same thing, just marked and unmarked, because you use the words "map" and "sketch." But -- oh, yeah. No, no objection. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right. That concludes the business with relation to this witness. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do have some -- some issues I would like to -- three issues I would like to raise concerning specifically this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The first issue I would like to raise, Mr. President, has to do with the question which was raised by the Trial Chamber at the beginning of this hearing when the Trial Chamber questioned the witness. We take issue with the second question which was -- answer which was posed by the Trial Chamber. We believe that there was -- the first question was entirely appropriate but that there is a difficulty with the second question. Because it places this Trial Chamber with an ethical dilemma. The witness answered differently, and I -- the question I refer to is at page 4, lines 11 to 18. When this question was posed to the witness, basically as to what happened in the office when he met with the Prosecution...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I object. I object to this submission completely and it should stop now. If he had any problem with the question he should have objected at the time -- or with the answer. This is -- the witness is gone now. There's -- the testimony is over. I don't understand how he can now take issue with any questions from the Bench, from me, or from anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- it was -- this was an issue that I could not interrupt the Trial Chamber when the Trial Chamber was questioning the witness and as you said yesterday, try and let the testimony flow. It was not the time to make this argument at that point. But when this second question raises an issue which the Trial Chamber must, in our opinion, be informed of. And there are consequences to the questions which go beyond what actually the question that was asked. And this is what I would like to raise with the Trial Chamber at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where are you leading us?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I am simply leading to the fact that the question that was posed to the witness about the meeting which took place between the witness and the Prosecution, this question put the witness into the -- the situation where he gave an answer which is different from what was put on paper by my colleague and what was -- what was said by my colleague to the Trial Chamber. We now have two different answers as to what happened in that room. The result of this, Mr. President, is that we have three choices: The first choice would be that the Prosecution lied. And never would anybody say that. So then maybe the witness lied, in which case he is a liar and all of his testimony must not be considered. But there is a third option. And the third option is, when that answer -- nobody lied, everybody told the truth, but actually the witness was put under pressure in that room that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I again --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's a matter which must be raised before the Trial Chamber in consideration of the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I object to this, I'm sorry, complete nonsense. He could have at the time said, Your Honour, I don't think that's a good question or objected to the question. Inconsistencies in a witness's answers, if they're made by the Prosecution -- questions from the Prosecution, questions from the Defence, questions from the Bench, these are not always -- they are not always complete consistencies, and that's where the Trial Chamber comes in and weighs the evidence and decides what weight to give it and what weight to give which answers and focuses on the demeanour of the witness and their recollection and the transcript. And finally, this is a matter that my friend could have dealt with on cross-examination and could have gone into, but he didn't ask anything about it. So I would ask that this entire inappropriate line be stopped now, and if he wants to make his argument at the appropriate time in his final brief about how the Trial Chamber should treat this evidence, that's one thing. But there is no pressing issue which needs to be raised now, and it's also an illogical argument, this kind of trilogy of choices, and again asserting the witness was put under pressure. If he wanted to do something about the Trial Chamber's question, he should have objected to the question at the time, and it's not true that he couldn't have stopped at that point and said something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Nicholls. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may for just one minute, Your Honour, Mr. President, I would like to join the debate in part. We hear from the Prosecutor from time to time, we want to get to the truth and we've said it on a number of occasions. I think it's what disingenuous. I don't think it's silly that we raise the issue as to how witnesses who consistently not only are impeached but are inconsistent with their prior testimonies, they come and testify about events 10 and 12 years later and have specific recollections. The Prosecutor himself could have used a number of tactics that are available to them so that there is a transparency, so we know what the truth is. And that is precisely to have the witness execute or sign the statement, which they failed to do, not the Defence, or they could have tape-recorded the interview that they had, since they desire to have the truth and this transparency, they should have tape-recorded the interview with these witnesses, especially if they themselves consider them to be hostile. That is not done on most occasions; only when it suits the Prosecutor to tape record or have them execute the statement. It would have taken them no more than 15 minutes with the resources that they have to have those accommodations made. They have chosen instead to put themselves as potential witnesses in this case and to determine whether or not a witness said something to the Prosecutor or not, and I think that's what's unfair and that's what, quite frankly, as my learned friend calls silly or -- that's what they should have done. They should have taken that avenue which was available to them. And I do say this because there are many witnesses coming forward which will probably and in all likelihood share the same process as this witness did. So I invite the Prosecutor to, if they want to have the truth and an open process, simply tape-record the interview. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the Chamber made it sufficiently clear before putting the questions to the witness that -- the basis for the Chamber to put questions to the witness. And the Chamber's purpose was to try to clarify his evidence, and I believe the Chamber is fully capable of interpreting the evidence of the witness. Let's stop here. And before we break there's some -- are there any administrative matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do have additional issues I would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, you said three items.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Three items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Actually, there is a fourth one, but it is very short. The second item I would like to raise also deals with the ruling that was given by the Trial Chamber at the beginning of this hearing. And I quote now from lines 2 -- page 2, lines 1 to 6, and page 10, lines 9 to 11. And I paraphrase what was put by the Trial Chamber. The fact that it would be entirely appropriate and consistent with the concept that there is no property in the witness, that I can ask a witness what was discussed with the Prosecution, that there was absolutely no problem with that. And secondly, that for telling witnesses to tell the truth when testifying in these circumstances do not constitute instances of pressuring the witness. I believe, Mr. President, my arguments were not held -- withheld by the Trial Chamber. I understand that. I made a common sense argument. I don't believe that there is a problem with that, but that Trial Chamber decided to reject this. I seek leave at this time to brief the issue. I feel this is an issue that is of major importance, what can be done with a witness when I meet a witness, whether I can ask him a question as to what did the Prosecution tell you and what kind of situation that puts the witness in. The second issue is through all my years I've always said that a person in authority telling a witness in circumstances like this to say, "You have to tell the truth" several occasion in the same interview, Trial Chamber might believe that this is not putting pressure on a witness. I believe otherwise, and I will produce the case law that says that the person in authority saying to a witness that he has to tell the truth on many occasions in a short period of time, I will produce the case law which says that legally this is unwise and unsound. More importantly, Mr. President, I do believe that by doing these things, we are playing with the witnesses, which is what we want to avoid. These witnesses are under hardship when they come here and they should not be played around with this way. That's why I just simply seek leave to brief the issue in law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We object to this, Your Honour. I think -- I think we should learn to live with the Court's judgements. There is no reason to -- for this to be written down anywhere, especially since the bulk of the argument appears to be factual challenges to the credibility of the Prosecution. I don't think you need to hear any more of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I hear your third point as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Third point also relates to the testimony of this witness. Mr. President, we -- you have heard from my cross-examination and also from my arguments dealing with what happened with this witness, I would like to ask that the Prosecution make its case precise against my client. The Prosecution has provided information to the Defence that he was not seen in Rocevic. The Prosecution has provided information to the Defence that he was not driven by his driver that day. The Prosecution has provided evidence to the Defence in a duty book that he was on duty at the Standard, or at the Zvornik Brigade command that day. The Prosecution has provided evidence to the Defence of a handwriting analysis that he was the one writing in the book that day in Zvornik Brigade command. Now, then they produce a witness to try to say that he is in Rocevic that day. I would like the Prosecution to tell what is it -- what is the case I have to meet? Is my client alleged to have been in Rocevic that day, is my client alleged to have been in Zvornik command, or is my client alleged to have everything all wrong and that he falsified the book with the handwriting analysis, or that he wrote the book, he went to Rocevic, and he came back? I'd like to know the case I have to meet, and this will avoid many of these situations that we have lived with with this witness. If the Prosecution knew what its case was, it would be much easier for the Defence to face that case, and I'd would like to obtain some precision in this regard. What is the Prosecution's case regarding Drago Nikolic on the 15th of July. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did the Prosecution not make his -- its case clear by the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Certainly not clear in terms of what the evidence they will lead. They are leading contradictory evidence. Their case is not clear at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I welcome the chance to give you argument on what the case is. And I've offered that several times. No one has taken me up on it. Mr. Bourgon's -- likes to argue his case whenever he gets the chance, and he and I will argue everyone's case, if he wants us to. I think the indictment is clear, the brief is clear. I wouldn't expect all the evidence to be the same and non-contradictory, nor would the Trial Bench, but I can respond to all this, I can make the case clear. And the only reason I ask that is because it's a long case and it may help the Court in that respect. So I have no problem arguing these things and taking the time to do it. But it's really of course inappropriate unless the Court wants to sanction a practise like that. But we did it in the last trial I was in, and I think the Chamber found it was helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On the second issue the Chamber made a ruling, and the Chamber does not need a further brief on this matter. On the third issue, given that we are sitting pursuant to 15 bis, I think there may be some appropriate time in the conduct of the trial for -- to have argument or submissions to hear the cases. Any further administrative matters? Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do have one. I've asked my learned friend on a couple of occasions, both this week and I believe last week, for an estimate or reasonable estimate as to the duration of his case. And I'm wondering if the Court knows what that estimate is, because we were given estimates in July and August of last year as to what that is, and it's important for the Defence as well as for many other things. We're not tying him to that, but I think it's clear that the estimate given by Court and the Prosecutor of 11 and a half months doesn't seem to be realistic. And for many different reasons we'd like to see what the estimate of the duration of the Prosecutor's case is at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That is helpful. Mr. McCloskey, whether we can have an updated estimate after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That -- we have -- and we have been in discussions, because it is so important to everyone. We will take another look at our estimates that we -- actually wasn't that long ago, I think, that we filed something with estimates. As you know, our biggest problem in estimating is -- is estimating cross-examination times. This is where this case will get a bit longer or a bit shorter, and so we will give you our updated estimates, and we will have to see what -- what comes of the cross-examination. But that's -- that's the difficulty that we're in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, what the Chamber likes to have is the overall time necessary for the presentation of the Prosecution's evidence, which will take for the examination-in-chief, excluding the time for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's no problem. That's -- that's no problem, and you -- we can all add it up what's in the record now, from our previous filings if we subtract the witnesses. And we have made a brief -- if we do that, we have 177.5 hours left and 82 live witnesses to go, and we're about halfway through. But we're going to take a good look at this, see if we can knock people off, see if our estimates are okay, and try to give you a better -- a better estimate so that we can all plan our lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, we were informally informed that in relation to three witnesses you are going to convert into 92 ter witnesses. Two of them, as for two of them you changed the position to call them live. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We had -- you recall Mr. Haynes had entered discussions with us about three. We looked at it initially and we agreed with one. I looked at it again last night because I had been reminded that we hadn't provided you with the statements. And I thought that Mr. Haynes probably had a point on the second one as well. So we've -- we're on our way in providing you with -- oh, it's already been done -- with the remaining statement of the witness that we will have as 92 ter. That's where we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's just to clarify, 132 and 108 are viva voce and 117 is 92 ter, which is Ms. Stewart's conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will make a ruling as soon as possible after having reference to that 92 ter statement. Mr. Nicholls or Mr. Bourgon. Who's first? Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think I -- just if I can assist my friend, Your Honour, Mr. Bourgon, Your Honour, asked about the indictment. I'd suggest my friend read paragraph 30.8.1, which is headed, Rocevic school and states Drago Nikolic and Milorad Trbic travelled to the Rocevic school to supervise the VRS personnel guarding the prisoners, which might help him with our case, whether or not we were saying that Drago Nikolic went to the school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I won't comment on the fact that they've got all kinds of contradictory evidence, but that's not the point I'd like to raise, Mr. President. I would -- administrative matter which is that on the 9th of March we were served with a handwriting analysis expert report, and according to the dead-line set, we normally have to file our response to this report within 30 days, which would be by the 9th of April. We kindly ask Mr. President for a delay to respond, and until the 23rd of April. The reason for this delay is we are presently considering this handwriting analysis and maybe there won't be a need to challenge the expert report, and I think the additional time that we will take to carefully analyse whether we want to object or not, or cross-examine or not, this expert, warrants the delay, the short delay that we ask to produce our response by the 23rd of April, which is one week after the court recess. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It's granted. Then I don't think that we will have the next witness today. So court is adjourned. I hope everybody has a happy break, and we will adjourn [sic] on -- at 9.00 on the 16th.
